HR@10 against 99 sampled negatives measures performance within that candidate protocol; it does not establish full-catalog ranking quality. Krichene and Rendle show sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation. Keep the pinned evaluator unchanged and explicitly label results as sampled HR@10 with 99 unique negatives and evaluation seed 42. [On Sampled Metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/).

For uncertainty, adapt paired bootstrap resampling: retain each user’s hit indicator for both models, resample identical user indices within each category, recompute category means, then average the four means equally. Report the observed macro HR@10 difference and a 95% bootstrap interval, alongside category scores. Pairing preserves within-user comparisons; stratification preserves the benchmark’s category weighting. This is a proposed application of [paired bootstrap](https://aclanthology.org/W04-3250/). With 200 users/category, one changed hit moves category HR by 0.005 and macro HR by 0.00125. Intervals capture user-sampling uncertainty conditional on fixed candidates and trained models; they exclude training-seed and negative-sampling variability.

Repeatedly maximizing validation HR across checkpoints and trials introduces selection optimism; bootstrapping the selected winner on the same validation users does not remove it. Prespecify checkpoint evaluation frequency, stopping rules, trial limits, and deterministic tie-breaking; log every evaluated checkpoint and comparison. Treat validation intervals as descriptive after selection, avoid significance claims from tiny winning margins, and freeze the complete selection procedure before independent held-out evaluation. These controls follow the model-selection concerns in [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html), while preserving the fixed splits and evaluator.
